heading: Adivasi land, and the fight to keep it
body: Jharkhand, like Chhattisgarh, is a young state built from an old region: it was carved out of southern Bihar on 15 November 2000, under the Bihar Reorganisation Act, after a political movement for a separate tribal state that had been building since at least 1938, when the former hockey captain Jaipal Singh Munda founded the Adivasi Mahasabha to press the case. Roughly a quarter of Jharkhand's population today is Adivasi (Scheduled Tribe) — Munda, Santhal, Oraon and Ho communities chiefly, among many others — and it is their resistance to outside control, more than any dynastic history, that defines the region's past.

That resistance has a long documented record. The Santhal rebellion (Hul) of 1855–56, led by the brothers Sido and Kanhu Murmu, was a large-scale armed uprising against British land revenue policy and moneylenders across what is now Jharkhand and parts of Bengal. Four decades later came the Munda Rebellion (Ulgulan, or 'Great Tumult') of 1899–1900, led by Birsa Munda — still revered locally as Dharti Aba, 'Father of the Earth' — against British policies that had dismantled the Khuntkatti system of communal tribal landholding and handed land to outside landlords and moneylenders. Birsa Munda died in British custody in 1900 at around 25, but the rebellion he led is credited with pushing colonial authorities toward the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act, which gave some legal protection to tribal land rights.

The other defining thread is mineral wealth: the coalfields of Dhanbad-Jharia and the steel and mining belt around Bokaro and Jamshedpur made this one of colonial and independent India's most industrially important regions, developed from the late 19th century onward largely through migrant labour that displaced the same tribal communities from the land they had fought to protect. The places on this map reflect that layered history — a region whose Adivasi identity and its industrial economy grew up in tension with each other, and whose statehood is barely a generation old.
